role_context: A Docker & Java engineer at advanced proficiency is expected to independently design, build, containerize, and operate production-grade Java services, owning complex work such as Spring-based service architecture, JVM tuning, secure Docker image construction, CI/CD pipelines, and runtime observability. Day to day, they diagnose application and container issues across the full stack—from Java concurrency, GC behavior, ORM/query performance, and API reliability to Docker networking, storage, image layers, resource limits, and security policies. They should be trusted to define container standards, optimize build and deployment workflows, implement scanning/signing/SBOM practices, and make sound trade-offs around performance, maintainability, cost, and compliance with limited senior guidance. They also review critical designs and code, mentor less experienced engineers, and convert production incidents or platform risks into durable improvements such as runbooks, reusable base images, automated checks, and architecture guidelines.
questions_prompt:
Please ensure the questions you ask cover the key functional, logical, architectural, implementation, debugging, optimization, review, and problem-solving areas from the competency scope for {name}, matched to {proficiency} proficiency ({yoe} years experience).

Focus the assessment on applied Docker & Java work items that reflect real engineering scenarios. Do not ask trivia, pure syntax, framework setup, installation, configuration lookup, or testing-framework questions. The task should require the candidate to reason through requirements, constraints, tradeoffs, risks, edge cases, implementation quality, debugging signals, and pragmatic improvements.

This is a basic proficiency, so the tasks need to match one year of experience only. Somebody with one year of experience does not have extensive production experience and their concepts are usually shaky, so the complexity of the task needs to be basic only. Let the candidate be able to finish this within 15 minutes.

Relevant competency areas and sub-skills to cover, excluding testing frameworks, tool installation/setup, language/library syntax, and pure semantics:

Docker topic areas:
- Mental model of the container stack: Docker CLI, Docker daemon, container runtime, OCI concepts, Linux namespaces, cgroups, and how container isolation works at a practical level.
- Image internals and lifecycle reasoning: image layers, manifests, content-addressable storage, layer reuse, image size implications, and cleanup/garbage-collection considerations.
- Image construction and build engineering: multi-stage builds, reproducible builds, deterministic image contents, image optimization, build cache usage, build metadata, multi-platform image considerations, and avoiding leaking secrets into images.
- Base image strategy: minimal vs. full images, distro choice, image hardening, vulnerability remediation, SBOM/provenance awareness, and auditable image supply chains.
- Registry and image distribution concerns: private registry usage, retention policies, replication/mirroring concepts, image tag immutability, promotion between environments, and reliability of image delivery.
- Container networking design and troubleshooting: bridge, overlay, host, none, MACVLAN/IPVLAN concepts; service discovery; embedded DNS; load balancing; ingress routing; network isolation; packet flow; MTU implications; IPv4/IPv6 awareness; and diagnosing connectivity issues using logs and network evidence.
- Container storage and filesystem behavior: storage drivers such as overlay2/fuse-overlayfs/devicemapper/ZFS/Btrfs at a conceptual level, copy-on-write tradeoffs, bind mounts, volumes, tmpfs, remote storage, backup/restore needs, encryption-at-rest, durability, portability, inode pressure, and I/O performance implications.
- Runtime security and compliance: least privilege containers, rootless execution, capability trimming, read-only filesystems, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, masked paths, user namespace remapping, secret handling, credential rotation, image scanning, policy gates, compliance benchmarks, and software supply-chain assurance.
- Orchestration and distributed operations: Docker Compose/Stack concepts, Swarm/Kubernetes/Nomad/ECS integration awareness, service primitives, rolling updates, rollback behavior, health orchestration, placement constraints, failure domains, node lifecycle, high availability, zero-downtime upgrades, and multi-region failover concepts.
- Observability, debugging, and performance tuning: per-container CPU, memory, block I/O, network, PID, and OOM metrics; Docker event stream; structured logging; trace correlation; incident analysis using container exec/debug, namespace inspection, process tracing, cgroup pressure analysis, core dumps, and layer checksum validation; resource controls such as CPU shares, cpuset, memory limits, blkio weights, hugepages, and ulimits.
- Continuous delivery and developer experience: image build-push-promote flows, immutable tags, semantic versioning, release channels, scanning/signing awareness, local development parity with production images/runtime flags, dependency proxies, build caches, parallel build strategies, and reducing developer friction.
- Architecture, governance, and best practices: microservices vs. monolith tradeoffs, sidecars vs. helper containers, service mesh implications, multi-tenancy boundaries, cost models, coding/container guidelines, review checklists, base-image lifecycle, deprecation processes, RFCs, capacity planning, cost optimization, risk assessment, incident postmortems, and converting learnings into standards and automation.
- Leadership and knowledge sharing: mentoring less experienced engineers, writing practical documentation, creating reusable Docker Compose files/base image templates/internal modules, evaluating container trends such as rootless Docker, buildpacks, WASM containers, eBPF-based isolation, stargz/nydus snapshotters, and communicating technical constraints to InfoSec, SRE, QA, compliance, and business stakeholders.

Java topic areas:
- Object-oriented design and code quality: inheritance, encapsulation, polymorphism, abstraction, cohesion, coupling, maintainability, and critiquing/refining designs that do not meet practical best practices.
- Advanced Java design concepts: applying generics in reusable designs, annotations and annotation-processing concepts, functional constructs such as streams/lambdas with readability and performance tradeoffs, and thoughtful migration between Java versions.
- Concurrency and multithreading: Java Memory Model concepts, thread safety, race conditions, deadlocks, concurrent utilities, CompletableFuture, ForkJoinPool, designing robust concurrent flows, and selecting appropriate concurrency strategies.
- Collections and data structures: choosing collections based on time/space complexity, memory sensitivity, large-scale processing needs, ordering, uniqueness, lookup behavior, and performance tradeoffs.
- JVM internals and memory management: garbage collector concepts, GC log interpretation, memory leak diagnosis, heap/metaspace sizing, runtime tuning, class loading behavior, classpath conflict diagnosis, bytecode/instrumentation concepts, and production performance implications.
- Application architecture and modular design: layered architectures, modular boundaries, loose coupling, high cohesion, dependency direction, and choosing appropriate module/service boundaries.
- Design patterns and enterprise patterns: Factory, Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Dependency Injection, Repository, CQRS, and selecting patterns based on constraints rather than applying patterns mechanically.
- Distributed systems and microservices: API gateways, load balancing, service discovery, distributed transactions, fault tolerance, circuit breakers, bulkheads, failure handling, retry/idempotency concerns, and service boundary tradeoffs.
- Integration and interoperability: REST, SOAP, messaging systems, asynchronous flows, JSON/XML/Avro-style data exchange concepts, compatibility, schema evolution, and upstream/downstream dependency management.
- Enterprise Java and framework reasoning: Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Spring Security, Spring Cloud concepts, Jakarta EE concepts, IoC, AOP, persistence abstractions, and choosing framework approaches based on project context.
- Persistence and database interaction: ORM behavior, lazy loading, second-level caching concepts, transaction handling, query optimization, N+1 query risks, data consistency, and performance impact of persistence decisions.
- Build and dependency reasoning: multi-module project structure, dependency graph risks, version conflicts, release profiles, artifact boundaries, and maintainable build organization without asking for exact build-tool syntax.
- Containerization and cloud deployment for Java: Dockerizing Java applications, image optimization, JVM-in-container considerations, cloud deployment readiness, Kubernetes/cloud platform operational concerns, and environment parity.
- Observability and production troubleshooting: application logs, metrics, distributed tracing, dashboard/alert interpretation, performance bottleneck investigation, error spike diagnosis, and correlating application behavior with infrastructure signals.
- Performance engineering: profiling CPU and memory hotspots, reducing GC overhead, diagnosing degradation, throughput vs. latency tradeoffs, caching strategies, serialization choices, realistic performance experiments, and proposing code-level or architectural optimizations.
- Security and compliance: secure coding, input validation, authentication/authorization design, injection prevention, encryption, hashing, secure session management, OAuth2/JWT/SAML concepts, role-based and permission-based access controls, OWASP Top 10 awareness, PCI-DSS/GDPR-style data-handling concerns, and practical security tradeoffs.
- Code review and maintainability: reviewing for correctness, readability, performance, reliability, security, extensibility, and maintainability; giving actionable feedback; and identifying hidden risks in existing implementations.
- Collaboration and architectural judgment: aligning technical solutions with business requirements, working with product/QA/operations/stakeholders, managing integrated-environment dependencies, balancing performance/reliability/maintainability, and guiding consistent standards.
- Continuous delivery and operational readiness: release readiness, deployment safety, environment promotion, rollback thinking, runtime configuration risks, operational runbooks, and production support considerations.

Assessment design guidance:
- Prefer a small realistic scenario such as reviewing a Dockerfile for a Java service, diagnosing a containerized Java application issue, improving a simple service deployment plan, reviewing a code/design snippet for concurrency or persistence risks, or proposing a safe operational fix for a failing containerized Java workload.
- Ask the candidate to explain assumptions, identify likely root causes, call out risks and edge cases, and propose a pragmatic fix or improvement.
- The task may include a short code snippet, Dockerfile, Compose fragment, log excerpt, metric snapshot, architecture note, or pull-request description, but it should be solvable by reasoning rather than memorizing commands or syntax.
- Keep the scenario bounded enough for completion within 15 minutes.
- Prioritize signal on practical judgment: does the candidate understand requirements and constraints, reason through ambiguity, make sound tradeoffs, identify risks, and improve an existing implementation realistically?
- Avoid questions that depend on exact command flags, exact framework annotations, installation steps, CI configuration syntax, unit-test framework details, or obscure trivia.

The goal is to evaluate applied competence, practical problem-solving, implementation and review ability, sound technical judgment, and the candidate's ability to deliver realistic solutions within the expected time constraints for their proficiency level.
